difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: the principle requires both (a) a product defect and (b) the consumer's non-contribution to the defect before compensation is warranted. Traps satisfy only one condition.
stimulus: A manufacturer is obligated to compensate a consumer for a product's failure if, and only if, the failure resulted from a defect in the product itself and the consumer did nothing that contributed to the defect.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A blender's motor burns out two weeks after purchase because the consumer regularly ran it without the lid, causing overheating. The manufacturer declines to compensate the consumer, even though an internal wiring flaw also contributed to the burnout.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A laptop's screen cracks after the owner drops it. The manufacturer refuses compensation, citing the drop as the cause, though an internal hinge defect had already weakened the screen before it was dropped.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A washing machine leaks on its first use due to a factory-installed seal that was never properly attached. The owner did nothing unusual during operation. The manufacturer compensates the owner.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A power tool's blade shatters because the consumer used it on material the manual warned against. The manufacturer compensates the consumer anyway, citing a secondary flaw in the blade's composition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A television set fails after a power surge during a storm. The manufacturer compensates the consumer, even though no product defect existed and the consumer had not purchased a surge protector.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies both conditions of the principle: (1) the failure resulted from a defect in the product itself (the factory-installed seal was never properly attached), and (2) the consumer did nothing that contributed to the defect (normal operation). The manufacturer's compensation therefore conforms to the principle.
explanations.A: Partial fit / violates principle. The consumer contributed to the defect by running the blender without a lid. The principle requires consumer non-contribution, so compensation is not warranted. The manufacturer declining is defensible, but the question asks which judgment conforms — this scenario muddies both conditions.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. A defect existed (the hinge flaw), but the consumer also contributed to the failure by dropping the laptop. Because the consumer contributed, the principle does not require compensation, making the manufacturer's refusal ambiguous rather than a clean conform.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. The consumer used the tool on warned-against material, contributing to the blade's failure. Even if a secondary flaw existed, the principle does not obligate compensation when the consumer contributed. Compensating here violates the principle.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope / violates principle. No product defect existed — the failure was due to an external power surge. The principle applies only when the failure results from a defect, so compensation here is not warranted and violates the principle.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent: a physician is justified in disclosing patient information only if (a) disclosure is necessary to prevent serious harm and (b) the patient has been informed that disclosure may occur. Traps satisfy only one part.
stimulus: A physician is justified in disclosing confidential patient information to a third party only if doing so is necessary to prevent serious harm to an identifiable person and the patient has been previously informed that such disclosure is possible.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A psychiatrist discloses to police that a patient has made credible threats against a coworker. The patient was told at intake that serious threats could be reported. The disclosure is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A physician informs a patient's employer that the patient has a communicable disease, having warned the patient in advance that health information might be shared. The disclosure is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A physician discloses a patient's mental health history to a family member, believing it will reduce the patient's stress, without ever having informed the patient that such disclosures could occur. The disclosure is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctor reveals a patient's diagnosis to a research team studying the disease, noting that the patient had consented generally to research use of records. The disclosure is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A physician discloses a patient's drug addiction to the patient's landlord to prevent the patient from being evicted, having warned the patient that addiction status could be shared in housing disputes. The disclosure is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) disclosure is necessary to prevent serious harm to an identifiable person (the threatened coworker), and (2) the patient was previously informed at intake that such disclosure could occur. The judgment that the disclosure is justified therefore conforms to the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit / scope mismatch. Informing the employer about a communicable disease may constitute serious harm prevention, but sharing employment-related health information is not clearly necessary to prevent harm to an identifiable person — it more closely resembles administrative disclosure. This choice is ambiguous on condition (1).
explanations.C: Violates the principle. The disclosure was not to prevent serious harm (stress reduction is not serious harm), and the patient was never informed disclosure was possible. Both conditions fail.
explanations.D: Outside the principle's scope. Research use of records is not about preventing serious harm to an identifiable person, so condition (1) is not satisfied. The general research consent does not bring it within the principle.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. The patient was warned, satisfying condition (2). However, preventing eviction does not constitute preventing 'serious harm to an identifiable person' in the sense the principle intends — the disclosure is to benefit the patient, not protect a third party from harm. Condition (1) fails.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in an ethics context: a person is blameworthy for an outcome only if (a) they foresaw it as likely and (b) they had a reasonable means of preventing it. Traps satisfy only one condition or confuse foreseeability with mere possibility.
stimulus: A person is morally blameworthy for a harmful outcome only if that person foresaw the outcome as a likely result of their action and had a reasonable means available by which they could have prevented it.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A contractor knew it was likely that using substandard fasteners would cause the balcony to collapse and could have purchased code-compliant fasteners at minimal extra cost, yet chose the substandard ones. The contractor is morally blameworthy for the collapse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A driver did not foresee that running a yellow light would cause an accident but could have easily stopped in time. The driver is morally blameworthy for the resulting collision.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hiker foresaw that the mountain trail was dangerous but had no alternative route and no means of rescue for an injured companion. The hiker is morally blameworthy for the companion's death.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A factory manager foresaw that emissions might possibly cause illness in nearby residents but installed the only available filtration technology. The manager is morally blameworthy for the residents' illnesses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A nurse foresaw that a medication error was a likely result of fatigue and had the reasonable option of requesting a shift handoff, but did not. A supervisor later caught the error before any harm resulted. The nurse is morally blameworthy for the near-miss.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) the contractor foresaw the collapse as a likely result (knew substandard fasteners would likely cause it), and (2) the contractor had a reasonable means of prevention (code-compliant fasteners at minimal cost) but did not use it. The judgment of blameworthiness conforms to the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. A reasonable means of prevention existed (stopping in time), but the driver did not foresee the accident as likely — running a yellow light is not typically foreseen as likely to cause a collision. Condition (1) fails.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The hiker may have foreseen danger, but no reasonable means of prevention was available. Condition (2) fails, so blameworthiness is not warranted under the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit / foreseeability mismatch. The manager foresaw illness as a mere possibility, not as likely. The principle requires foresight of likelihood. Additionally, the manager used the only available technology, so condition (2) also fails.
explanations.E: Scope mismatch / extra fact misdirection. No harm resulted, and the principle speaks to blameworthiness for a harmful outcome. Without an actual harmful outcome, the principle's consequent cannot apply.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in policy: a government subsidy is warranted only if (a) the industry cannot be profitable without it and (b) the industry provides a public good unavailable from the private market. Distractors satisfy only one part.
stimulus: A government subsidy for a private industry is warranted only if the industry cannot achieve profitability without public support and the industry provides a public good that the private market would otherwise fail to supply.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rural postal delivery network cannot break even without government support and provides mail service to remote communities that no private carrier finds profitable to serve. The government subsidizes it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A domestic semiconductor firm is profitable but faces foreign competition. Because semiconductors are critical to national infrastructure, the government subsidizes the firm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An opera company cannot survive without public funding. Because several private donors have offered to fund the company instead, the government declines to subsidize it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A passenger rail line cannot earn a profit and provides a public transportation alternative. Several private rail companies offer competing service on the same route. The government subsidizes it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A national park concession company runs at a loss and has asked for government support. Other private companies have expressed interest in operating the same concessions. The government subsidizes it.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) the rural postal network cannot achieve profitability without support (cannot break even), and (2) it provides a public good — mail service to remote communities — that the private market fails to supply (no private carrier finds it profitable). The government subsidy is therefore warranted under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The semiconductor firm is profitable without support, so condition (1) fails. Even if condition (2) were met, the principle requires both conditions.
explanations.C: Reversed application / violates principle. The opera company cannot survive without funding (condition 1 met), but private donors could supply the good, so condition (2) — private market failure — is not satisfied. The government's refusal is consistent with the principle, but the question asks which judgment conforms, and this scenario's conclusion is reached for reasons that still don't fully satisfy both conditions.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The rail line cannot earn a profit (condition 1 met), but competing private rail service exists on the same route, meaning the private market does supply the good. Condition (2) fails.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. The concession company operates at a loss (condition 1 potentially met), but other private companies want to operate the same concessions, so the private market does not fail to supply the good. Condition (2) fails.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in environmental science: a developer may be required to restore a habitat only if (a) the development directly caused measurable ecological harm and (b) restoration is technically feasible. Traps omit one condition.
stimulus: A developer may be legally required to restore a natural habitat only if the development activity directly caused measurable harm to that habitat and restoration of the habitat to its prior condition is technically feasible.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mining company's operations drained a wetland, destroying measurable populations of protected plant species. Environmental engineers confirm the wetland can be restored to its prior state. Regulators require the company to restore the wetland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A housing developer built on a former agricultural field. Though no native habitat previously existed there, regulators require the developer to plant native species as habitat mitigation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A logging company cleared an old-growth forest, causing measurable habitat loss. Scientists determine that old-growth ecosystems cannot be restored on any human timescale. Regulators require full restoration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An industrial plant's runoff polluted a river, but tests show no measurable ecological harm to date. Because restoration is technically feasible, regulators require the plant to restore the riverbed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A resort developer cleared a coastal dune. Because the dune cannot be restored to its prior condition, regulators require the developer to create a new dune elsewhere as compensation.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) the mining operations directly caused measurable harm (destruction of protected plant populations), and (2) restoration is technically feasible (confirmed by engineers). The legal requirement to restore therefore conforms to the principle.
explanations.B: Outside the principle's scope. No natural habitat existed prior to development, so no measurable harm to a natural habitat occurred. Condition (1) fails entirely.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. Measurable habitat loss occurred (condition 1 met), but restoration to prior condition is not technically feasible on any human timescale. Condition (2) fails, so the requirement to restore violates the principle rather than conforming to it.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. Restoration is feasible (condition 2 met), but no measurable ecological harm has occurred. Condition (1) fails, so requiring restoration does not conform to the principle.
explanations.E: Partial fit / violates principle. The development caused harm (condition 1 likely met), but restoration to prior condition is not feasible. Condition (2) fails, and requiring a compensatory dune elsewhere — rather than restoration — does not conform to the principle's specific requirement.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in technology/law: an employee's personal communications may be monitored by an employer only if (a) the employee was clearly notified in advance and (b) the communications were conducted on employer-owned equipment. Distractors miss one part.
stimulus: An employer is justified in monitoring an employee's personal communications only if the employee was clearly notified in advance that such monitoring might occur and the communications were conducted using employer-owned equipment or networks.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A company's employee handbook, signed by all staff, states that messages sent via company computers may be monitored. A manager reviews personal emails an employee sent using the office desktop. The monitoring is justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An employee uses a personal smartphone on the company's Wi-Fi network to send private messages. The company monitors those messages, though no policy notifying employees of such monitoring exists. The monitoring is justified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An employer suspects an employee of leaking trade secrets and monitors the employee's personal cell phone messages, even though the cell phone is the employee's own device and no monitoring policy was disclosed. The monitoring is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An employee was informed during onboarding that personal calls made on company phones could be reviewed, but later makes those calls on a personal phone at home. The employer monitors the home phone. The monitoring is justified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A company clearly posts its monitoring policy in the employee lounge. An employee who never read the notice uses a company laptop to send personal messages. The employer monitors those messages. The monitoring is justified.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) the employee was clearly notified in advance — the handbook was signed by all staff, and (2) the communications were conducted on employer-owned equipment — the office desktop. The monitoring is therefore justified under the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The company's Wi-Fi is arguably employer-owned infrastructure (condition 2 debatable), but no policy notifying employees of monitoring exists. Condition (1) clearly fails.
explanations.C: Both conditions fail. No monitoring policy was disclosed (condition 1 fails) and the device is the employee's own (condition 2 fails). The monitoring is unjustified under the principle.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The employee was notified about company phones (condition 1 met for that context), but the monitoring targets a personal phone at home — not employer-owned equipment. Condition (2) fails.
explanations.E: Reversed application / partial fit. The employee used employer-owned equipment (condition 2 met), but posting a notice in a lounge the employee never read does not constitute clearly notifying the employee in advance. Condition (1) is not satisfied.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in economics: a price increase is exploitative only if (a) it occurs during a declared emergency and (b) the increase exceeds what is needed to cover increased supply costs. Traps satisfy only one condition.
stimulus: A price increase for an essential good is exploitative only if the increase occurs during a declared public emergency and the magnitude of the increase exceeds what is necessary to cover the seller's increased costs of supply.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During a declared flood emergency, a hardware store doubles the price of generators. The store's supply costs have not increased at all. A consumer advocate concludes the price increase is exploitative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During a declared flu epidemic, a pharmacy raises the price of antiviral medication by exactly the amount its wholesale costs increased. A regulator concludes the price increase is exploitative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A grocery store raises bread prices by 40 percent during a period of unusually high demand unrelated to any emergency. Supply costs have not risen. A regulator concludes the price increase is exploitative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: During a declared hurricane emergency, a fuel supplier raises prices by an amount equal to its increased transport costs. A consumer group concludes the price increase is exploitative.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A bottled-water company raises prices tenfold during normal market conditions after a competitor exits the market. Its supply costs are unchanged. A regulator concludes the price increase is exploitative.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) the increase occurs during a declared public emergency (the flood emergency), and (2) the increase exceeds what is necessary to cover increased supply costs — the store's costs have not increased at all, yet prices doubled. The conclusion that the increase is exploitative conforms to the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The emergency condition is met (declared flu epidemic), but the price increase equals exactly the increased wholesale costs — it does not exceed what is necessary to cover supply costs. Condition (2) fails, so the exploitative judgment does not conform.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. Supply costs have not risen, so condition (2) would be met. However, the price increase occurs during a period of high demand with no declared emergency. Condition (1) fails.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. A declared emergency exists (condition 1 met), but the price increase equals the increased transport costs — it does not exceed what is necessary. Condition (2) fails, so the exploitative conclusion does not conform.
explanations.E: Partial fit / outside scope. Supply costs are unchanged and the increase is large, satisfying condition (2). However, the price increase occurs during normal market conditions — no declared emergency. Condition (1) fails.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in law/evidence: a court should admit hearsay evidence only if (a) the declarant is unavailable to testify and (b) the statement was made under circumstances indicating its reliability. Traps satisfy only one part.
stimulus: A court is justified in admitting hearsay evidence only if the original declarant is unavailable to testify at trial and the statement was made under circumstances that provide adequate indications of its reliability.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A witness who recorded a dying person's account of the cause of her injury cannot testify because she has since died. The dying person's statement was made under the belief she would not survive. The court admits the statement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A declarant is unavailable because she refuses to travel to the courthouse. Her out-of-court statement was overheard at a party and written down by a bystander with no special knowledge of the events. The court admits the statement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A declarant is present at trial and ready to testify. His prior written statement was made to his attorney under oath. Because the statement is highly reliable, the court admits it as hearsay.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A business record contains an employee's statement about a transaction. The employee is available to testify but is not called. Because business records are typically reliable, the court admits the record as hearsay.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A deceased expert's written report is submitted as hearsay. The report was prepared hastily and later acknowledged by the expert's colleagues to contain methodological errors. The court admits the report because the expert is unavailable.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) the original declarant (the dying person) is unavailable to testify — she has died, and (2) the statement was made under circumstances indicating reliability — a dying declaration made under the belief of imminent death is a classic reliability indicator. The court's admission conforms to the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit trap. The declarant is unavailable (condition 1 met), but the statement was overheard at a party by an uninvolved bystander with no special knowledge — the circumstances do not provide adequate reliability indications. Condition (2) fails.
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The statement was made under oath (condition 2 met for reliability), but the declarant is present and ready to testify. Condition (1) — unavailability — fails entirely.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. Business records may be reliable (condition 2 arguably met), but the employee is available to testify and simply was not called. Condition (1) fails.
explanations.E: Partial fit / violates principle. The declarant is unavailable (condition 1 met), but the report contains acknowledged methodological errors and was prepared hastily — the circumstances do not provide adequate reliability indications. Condition (2) fails, and admission violates the principle.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in history/policy: a government is justified in restricting access to historical records only if (a) disclosure would endanger identifiable living individuals and (b) the restriction is limited to the minimum period necessary. Traps satisfy one part or confuse scope.
stimulus: A government is justified in restricting public access to historical records only if releasing those records would pose a direct danger to identifiable living individuals and the period of restriction extends no longer than necessary to eliminate that danger.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A government restricts access to intelligence files that name foreign informants who are still alive and could be targeted if identified. The restriction is lifted as soon as those informants die or are safely relocated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government withholds wartime census records for seventy-two years because they contain data about ethnic minorities, citing historical sensitivity, even though no living individuals are endangered by their release.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A government restricts access to trial records from a political prosecution because their release would embarrass current officials. The restriction is set to last twenty-five years regardless of any danger to individuals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A government releases all medical records from a past epidemic immediately, even though several named patients are still alive and have specifically asked that their diagnoses remain private.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government restricts access to diplomatic cables that name living ambassadors who could face danger if exposed. The restriction is set to last one hundred years as a blanket policy, far exceeding the expected lifespans of those named.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) release would endanger identifiable living individuals (foreign informants who could be targeted), and (2) the restriction is limited to the minimum period necessary — it is lifted as soon as those individuals die or are safely relocated. The restriction therefore conforms to the principle.
explanations.B: Partial fit / outside scope. No living individuals are endangered by the release of the census records, so condition (1) fails entirely. The restriction is not justified under the principle regardless of the period.
explanations.C: Both conditions fail. The restriction is motivated by official embarrassment, not danger to identifiable living individuals (condition 1 fails). Additionally, a fixed twenty-five-year period regardless of actual danger does not satisfy the minimum-necessary requirement (condition 2 also questionable).
explanations.D: Violates the principle. Living named patients could be endangered or harmed by involuntary disclosure (condition 1 arguably met), yet the government releases records immediately without restriction — failing to apply a justified restriction when one is warranted.
explanations.E: Partial fit trap. Living ambassadors could face danger (condition 1 met), but the restriction is a blanket one-hundred-year policy far exceeding the expected lifespans of those named — clearly not the minimum period necessary. Condition (2) fails.

difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent in arts/ethics: a critic is entitled to publish a negative review of an unpublished work only if (a) the work was shared with the critic by the author for the purpose of obtaining feedback and (b) the review does not disclose the work's content beyond what is necessary to support the critique. Traps satisfy only one part.
stimulus: A critic is entitled to publish a negative review of an author's unpublished work only if the author voluntarily shared the work with the critic for the purpose of obtaining critical feedback and the review refrains from disclosing the work's content beyond what is necessary to support the critique.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An author sends a manuscript to a critic and asks for honest critical assessment before seeking a publisher. The critic publishes a negative review that quotes only the passages necessary to illustrate its structural weaknesses. The publication is entitled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An author shares a draft novel with a friend who happens to be a critic. The author shared the draft for personal encouragement, not critical feedback. The critic publishes a negative review revealing the novel's entire plot. The publication is entitled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critic obtains a leaked copy of an unpublished manuscript without the author's knowledge. The review is sharply negative but carefully limits quotation to what is needed to support the critique. The publication is entitled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An author asks a critic for feedback and receives it privately. The critic then publishes a negative review that reproduces the manuscript's first three chapters in their entirety, far beyond what the critique requires. The publication is entitled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critic is given an unpublished play by the playwright for feedback. The critic publishes a glowing positive review that quotes extensively from the script. The publication is entitled.

explanations.correct: Choice A satisfies both conditions: (1) the author voluntarily shared the manuscript with the critic for the purpose of obtaining critical feedback, and (2) the review limits disclosure to passages necessary to illustrate structural weaknesses — no excess content is revealed. The publication is therefore entitled under the principle.
explanations.B: Both conditions fail. The author shared the draft for personal encouragement, not critical feedback (condition 1 fails). Additionally, the critic reveals the entire plot — far beyond what is necessary (condition 2 fails).
explanations.C: Partial fit trap. The review limits quotation to what is needed (condition 2 met), but the critic obtained the manuscript without the author's knowledge — it was not voluntarily shared for the purpose of critical feedback. Condition (1) fails.
explanations.D: Partial fit trap. The author asked for feedback (condition 1 met), but the review reproduces three entire chapters, far beyond what the critique requires. Condition (2) fails.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope. The principle governs negative reviews. A glowing positive review falls outside the principle entirely — the principle does not address whether positive reviews of shared work are entitled, so the judgment cannot conform.
